nameStory: The 'dwarf' in this mussel's name comes from its petite size compared to other freshwater mussels - it's one of the smallest in New England. The 'wedge' refers to its triangular, wedge-like shell shape when viewed from the side, while 'mussel' comes from the Old English 'muscle,' referring to the strong muscular foot these animals use to burrow.
description: The Dwarf Wedgemussel is a tiny freshwater clam that lives buried in clean river and stream bottoms. This critically endangered species has a smooth, triangular shell that's typically yellowish-brown to dark brown in color. Adults reach only about 1.5 inches long, making them one of the smallest mussels in New England. Like other freshwater mussels, they filter water through their bodies to catch microscopic food particles.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Extremely small for a mussel - only about 1 to 1.5 inches long when fully grown, roughly the size of a large marble

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly triangular or wedge-shaped when viewed from the side, with a pointed front end and rounded back end

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Smooth shell ranging from yellowish-brown to dark chocolate brown, often with faint growth rings visible

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Feels smooth to the touch with a slightly glossy surface, lacking the bumps or ridges found on many other mussel species

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Found only in exceptionally clean, fast-flowing streams with sandy or gravelly bottoms - their presence indicates pristine water quality

habitat: Dwarf Wedgemussels require crystal-clear, fast-flowing streams and small rivers with sandy or fine gravel bottoms. They're extremely sensitive to pollution and are found only in the cleanest waterways, typically in areas with good tree cover that keeps water temperatures cool. In New England, they're known from just a handful of pristine stream systems.

seasonality.spring: Best time to spot them as spring floods may expose shells along stream edges. Look for their small triangular shells among larger mussel shells after high water recedes.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're filtering water and growing. Empty shells may wash up on sandy stream banks during low water periods in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Still active but harder to find as they burrow deeper in preparation for winter. Fresh shells may appear after autumn storms.
seasonality.winter: Buried deep in stream sediments and nearly impossible to find. Look for empty shells that ice has pushed onto banks during winter thaws.

funFact: This tiny mussel is so rare that it was thought to be extinct in New England for decades until a small population was rediscovered - finding one is like discovering a living fossil in your local stream!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with juvenile Eastern Elliptio mussels, but young Elliptios are more oval-shaped rather than distinctly triangular. Remember: if it's wedge-shaped AND tiny (under 2 inches), it might be this rare species - but don't disturb it!
contextualKnowledge: This is one of North America's most endangered freshwater mussels, protected under the Endangered Species Act. If you think you've found one, observe but don't collect - even touching them can harm these fragile creatures that are barely hanging on in New England's waterways.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in New England, compare it to other small freshwater mussels like the Eastern Elliptio. The Dwarf Wedgemussel is much smaller and more triangular than any Elliptio species. Unlike the common Alewife Floater, it has a smooth shell without pronounced growth ridges and lives in flowing water rather than still ponds.
